title: From objective discovery to prediction of global ocean eco-provinces: A pathway for trustworthy learning
summary: Marine ecosystems are increasingly impacted by climate change, necessitating tools to identify and predict spatial habitat information. To build such tools, ecological marine provinces, "eco-provinces", ecologically meaningful regions in the global ocean can be used. We use unsupervised machine learning (ML) to identify eco-provinces with corresponding uncertainty measures based on output of a global simulation of phytoplankton functional types. Our work aims to create a proof of concept to predict eco-provinces based on satellite ocean color data. To do so, we develop a hierarchy of explainable dense ensemble networks to infer how well the eco-provinces can be detected from modeled ocean color fields. Key results include that the delineated eco-provinces are both ecologically meaningful and can be inferred with high skill. However, no straightforward relationship was found where adding more input data to the network consistently improves inference skill, and there is an intricate tradeoff between inputs and prediction fidelity. Our work is a case for optimism and a cautionary tale of needing uncertainty quantification and careful validation of prediction fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper uses unsupervised ML to define ecologically meaningful marine "eco-provinces" with uncertainty measures, then develops explainable dense ensemble networks to predict these provinces from ocean color data, showing high inference skill but a non-trivial input/fidelity tradeoff.
AI.motivation: Marine ecosystems face growing climate change impacts, creating a need for tools to identify and predict spatial habitat information, with eco-provinces serving as ecologically meaningful regions for such tools.
AI.method: Unsupervised ML identifies eco-provinces with uncertainty measures from a global simulation of phytoplankton functional types; a hierarchy of explainable dense ensemble networks infers eco-provinces from modeled ocean color fields, serving as a proof of concept for satellite-based prediction.
AI.result: Delineated eco-provinces are ecologically meaningful and can be inferred with high skill, but adding more input data does not consistently improve inference skill, revealing an intricate input–fidelity tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: The work offers both optimism and caution, highlighting the necessity of uncertainty quantification and careful validation of prediction fidelity.

title: Planning as Dynamics Relaxation: Hippocampal Recurrent Network Realizes Optimal Goal-Directed Navigation
summary: Neural correlates of spatial cognitive map are well documented, yet exactly how neural circuits perform spatial navigation in complex environments - e.g., reaching a goal while avoiding obstacles - remains largely unclear. Here, we show that a hippocampal network with appropriate recurrent connections can naturally achieve optimal goal-directed navigation via its relaxation dynamics. Specifically, we consider that the recurrent weights between the neurons represent the transition probabilities between spatial locations encoded by neurons; obstacles such as walls and blocked corridors are therefore reflected by the vanishing of connection weights. This connection pattern can be learned in the hippocampus via behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) while the animal is exploring the environment. When a goal signal is presented, the network dynamics will relax into an activity field representing the goal location. We prove that this field is mathematically equivalent to the desirability field of a Linearly-solvable Markov Decision Process (LMDP), and the local log-gradient of the field indicates the navigation direction. Both theoretical analyses and simulations demonstrate that this recurrent network dynamics-mediated navigation is efficient and robust in environments with complex obstacle layouts. Moreover, only low-rank updates of the network's connection pattern are needed when the environment has local changes. We hope this study offers insight into a general circuit principle for planning in abstract rational maps in the brain beyond spatial navigation.

AI.tldr: A hippocampal recurrent network, with weights encoding spatial transition probabilities, achieves optimal goal-directed navigation via relaxation dynamics equivalent to the LMDP desirability field.
AI.motivation: Spatial cognitive map correlates are known, but how neural circuits actually perform navigation in complex environments (reaching a goal while avoiding obstacles) remains unclear.
AI.method: Model a hippocampal network whose recurrent weights represent transition probabilities between locations; obstacles correspond to vanishing weights. Weights are learned via behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) during exploration. A goal signal makes the network relax into an activity field, proven equivalent to the desirability field of a Linearly-solvable Markov Decision Process (LMDP), with local log-gradient indicating direction.
AI.result: Theory and simulations show navigation is efficient and robust in complex obstacle layouts; only low-rank updates of the connection pattern are needed for local environmental changes.
AI.conclusion: Suggests a general circuit principle for planning in abstract rational maps in the brain beyond spatial navigation.

title: Chemical and geometric representation fidelity improves drug--target affinity prediction
summary: Predicting drug--target binding affinity (DTA) requires models to distinguish subtle chemical and structural determinants underlying molecular recognition. Although recent approaches increasingly incorporate richer drug and protein information, such information may be compressed, homogenized or discretized during representation construction, causing affinity-relevant distinctions to be lost before interaction modelling. We hypothesized that this representation-stage information loss constitutes an upstream bottleneck that cannot be reliably overcome by increasingly complex interaction predictors. To test this hypothesis, we developed ReGeoDTA, a representation-preserving framework that maintains affinity-relevant chemical heterogeneity in molecular representations and continuous geometric relationships in protein structures. Across three benchmark datasets, ReGeoDTA consistently improved affinity prediction, and the proposed representation-preserving strategies retained their benefits across diverse DTA architectures. Controlled representation degradation progressively reduced predictive performance, whereas increasing downstream predictor complexity failed to recover information lost during representation construction. These findings identify representation fidelity as an upstream design principle for accurate and generalizable drug--target affinity prediction, with potential implications for computational compound prioritization.

AI.tldr: Representation-stage information loss is an upstream bottleneck in DTA prediction; ReGeoDTA preserves chemical heterogeneity and continuous protein geometry, improving affinity prediction where more complex interaction predictors cannot recover the lost information.
AI.motivation: Existing DTA models add richer drug/protein information, but representation construction may compress, homogenize, or discretize it, losing affinity-relevant distinctions before interaction modelling. The authors hypothesize this representation-stage information loss is an upstream bottleneck that complex interaction predictors cannot overcome.
AI.method: ReGeoDTA, a representation-preserving framework that maintains affinity-relevant chemical heterogeneity in molecular representations and continuous geometric relationships in protein structures.
AI.result: Across three benchmark datasets, ReGeoDTA consistently improved affinity prediction; the representation-preserving strategies retained benefits across diverse DTA architectures. Controlled representation degradation progressively reduced performance, while increasing downstream predictor complexity failed to recover information lost during representation construction.
AI.conclusion: Representation fidelity is an upstream design principle for accurate and generalizable DTA prediction, with potential implications for computational compound prioritization.

title: Interstitial flow in the chick yolk sac exhibits organ-scale patterns driven by segregated leakage and drainage
comment: 27 pages, 10 figures, 1 table; includes Supplementary Materials
summary: Interstitial flow plays a key role in drug delivery, angiogenesis, cancer, and edema. Recent studies show that the interstitium can provide connected pathways capable of supporting long-distance material transport. However, the spatial scale of physiological interstitial flow remains unclear: despite the existence of connected pathways, flow may be dominated by nearby vascular filtration or extend over longer distances. Here, we identify organ-scale interstitial flow patterns in the chick yolk sac and elucidate the mechanisms that determine their spatial scale. The yolk sac serves as an organ-scale interstitial region that allows large-scale flow patterns to be identified without truncation. Our approach combines experimental imaging with computational modeling of coupled blood and interstitial flow in the whole yolk sac. Scaling analysis identifies a hydraulic conductivity ratio that controls the transition from small-scale to organ-scale flow. In organ-scale patterns, we find interstitial flow speed to be substantially greater than the transvascular flow speed. Mechanistically, the organ-scale patterns arise from the spatial segregation of the leakage and drainage of interstitial fluid from the vessels. These findings have important implications for biological transport by interstitial flow, suggesting that flow-mediated cues may be sensed locally but generated nonlocally.

AI.tldr: This study identifies organ-scale interstitial flow patterns in the chick yolk sac and reveals the mechanisms controlling their spatial scale, showing that flow-mediated cues may be sensed locally but generated nonlocally.
AI.motivation: The spatial scale of physiological interstitial flow remains unclear—despite connected interstitial pathways supporting long-distance transport, flow could be dominated by nearby vascular filtration or extend over longer distances.
AI.method: The authors combine experimental imaging with computational modeling of coupled blood and interstitial flow in the whole chick yolk sac, which serves as an untruncated organ-scale interstitial region. Scaling analysis identifies a hydraulic conductivity ratio governing the transition from small-scale to organ-scale flow.
AI.result: A hydraulic conductivity ratio controls the small-to-organ-scale flow transition. In organ-scale patterns, interstitial flow speed substantially exceeds transvascular flow speed, arising from spatial segregation of vessel leakage and drainage of interstitial fluid.
AI.conclusion: Organ-scale interstitial flow patterns exist and are governed by leakage-drainage segregation, implying that flow-mediated cues may be sensed locally but generated nonlocally, with implications for biological transport.

title: Polymerase-mediated quasispecies dynamics: bifurcations, complementation, and robustness of τ-tipping
summary: Quasispecies theory describes how mutation and selection shape highly variable RNA virus populations, but most models explicitly consider neither RNA-dependent RNA polymerases nor the delays associated with their synthesis and functional activation. A recent minimal model showed that delayed polymerase availability can induce extinction by reorganizing basins of attraction, a mechanism termed τ-tipping. Here, we extend this framework to a delay differential equation model in which master and mutant genomes encode distinct functional polymerases. We characterize its equilibrium and bifurcation structure, identifying master-mutant coexistence, mutant-only persistence (error catastrophe), and complete extinction governed by transcritical and saddle-node bifurcations. Although delays leave the equilibria unchanged, they reorganize their basins of attraction and can redirect populations that would otherwise persist at fixed mutation and replication parameters toward extinction, thereby extending τ-tipping to systems with autonomous mutant replication. We also recover the previously studied complementation model as a limiting case in which defective genomes depend on master-derived polymerase, providing a comprehensive analysis of the bifurcation structure. Comparing the two models shows that the ability of mutant genomes to encode functional polymerases determines whether loss of the master sequence results in mutant replacement or complete population extinction. The occurrence of delay-induced extinction in both settings demonstrates the robustness of τ-tipping and connects intracellular replication kinetics, complementation, and quasispecies extinction. Finally, we translate this mechanism into concrete virological predictions and propose experimental strategies to test the effects of replicase timing, RNA degradation, and functional complementation on viral persistence.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the τ-tipping framework via a delay differential equation model where master and mutant genomes encode distinct functional polymerases, showing delays can redirect persistent populations toward extinction and connecting replication kinetics, complementation, and quasispecies extinction.
AI.motivation: Quasispecies theory describes mutation and selection in RNA virus populations, but most models ignore RNA-dependent RNA polymerases and the delays in their synthesis and activation. A recent minimal model showed delayed polymerase availability can cause extinction by reorganizing basins of attraction (τ-tipping), but it did not address systems with autonomous mutant replication.
AI.method: The authors develop a delay differential equation model in which master and mutant genomes encode distinct functional polymerases, characterize its equilibrium and bifurcation structure (transcritical and saddle-node), and recover a prior complementation model as a limiting case where defective genomes depend on master-derived polymerase.
AI.result: They identify master-mutant coexistence, mutant-only persistence (error catastrophe), and complete extinction. Delays leave equilibria unchanged but reorganize basins of attraction, potentially driving otherwise-persistent populations to extinction, extending τ-tipping to systems with autonomous mutant replication.
AI.conclusion: Whether mutants can encode functional polymerases determines if loss of the master sequence yields mutant replacement or full extinction. Delay-induced extinction occurs in both settings, demonstrating τ-tipping robustness and linking intracellular replication kinetics, complementation, and quasispecies extinction, with concrete virological predictions and experimental strategies proposed.

title: SenSASP: A Unified, Multi-Layer Database of Senescence and SASP Genes
summary: Research on cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) draws on independently curated gene resources that differ in scope, identifiers, and update cycles, making cross-resource integration error-prone. We unified four widely used resources, CellAge, GenAge, the SenMayo signature, and the Reactome Cellular Senescence pathway, onto a single canonical identifier (the Ensembl gene ID) and enriched every gene with three annotation layers absent from all four inputs: cross-species conservation, tissue and cell-type expression, and high-confidence protein-protein interactions. Unification collapsed 1,460 summed source entries into 1,250 unique genes (210 redundant entries removed, 14.4%) while preserving full source provenance: 173 genes are corroborated by two or more resources and two (IL6, JUN) by all four. The three annotation layers reach 95.8%, 97.9%, and 93.0% of genes, with 89.4% annotated across all three. A 500-gene random sample of identifier mappings was validated against HGNC and Ensembl (98.0% exact match). The result, SenSASP, is a single, machine-readable, provenance-tracked database of harmonized identifiers and net-new functional context, illustrated here with a gene-prioritization score and a tissue-expression atlas. SenSASP is freely available at https://xuan13hao.github.io/sensasp/

AI.tldr: SenSASP is a unified, provenance-tracked database that harmonizes four major cellular senescence/SASP gene resources onto Ensembl gene IDs and adds conservation, expression, and PPI annotations.
AI.motivation: Cellular senescence and SASP research relies on independently curated gene resources (CellAge, GenAge, SenMayo, Reactome) that differ in scope, identifiers, and update cycles, making cross-resource integration error-prone.
AI.method: Unified the four resources onto the canonical Ensembl gene ID and enriched genes with three annotation layers: cross-species conservation, tissue/cell-type expression, and high-confidence protein-protein interactions. Validated 500 random identifier mappings against HGNC and Ensembl.
AI.result: Collapsed 1,460 source entries into 1,250 unique genes (210 redundant, 14.4% removed) with full provenance: 173 genes corroborated by ≥2 resources and IL6, JUN by all four. Annotation coverage reached 95.8%, 97.9%, 93.0%, and 89.4% across all three. Validation showed 98.0% exact match.
AI.conclusion: SenSASP provides a single machine-readable, provenance-tracked database of harmonized identifiers and net-new functional context, demonstrated via a gene-prioritization score and tissue-expression atlas; freely available online.

title: Sequential reduction for discrete latent variables in ecological and evolutionary models using RTMB
summary: Statistical models of ecological and evolutionary dynamics often include latent variables that are either continuous (e.g., average body size) or discrete (e.g., numerical abundance). Mixed-type hierarchical models containing both are typically fitted using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which can be prohibitively slow for large models. Here, we introduce an alternative in the R package RTMB that automates the sequential reduction of small groups of related discrete variables, allowing them to be efficiently marginalized. Sequential reduction is combined with automatic differentiation and the Laplace approximation to estimate parameters and predict both continuous and discrete variables. We demonstrate speed and flexibility using demographic examples (occupancy, dynamic occupancy, N-mixture, and open dynamic N-mixture models), benchmarking RTMB against JAGS and unmarked. We then develop two novel applications. The first is a multi-site open N-mixture model with a spatial latent variable governing site-specific initial abundance and recruitment, which shows that continuous Gaussian Markov random fields can be estimated jointly with discrete abundance dynamics in under a minute. The second is phylogenetic trait imputation for a published data set of female Liolaemus lizards, where we jointly impute a binary trait (viviparity), estimate its state-switching rates, and estimate its effect on a continuous trait (body size) during ancestral state reconstruction. This indicates that phylogenetic comparative methods can estimate linkages among discrete and continuous traits. We envision that intuitive and efficient specification of mixed-type models will allow more expressive representation of ecological and evolutionary dynamics.

AI.tldr: RTMB enables fast, automated marginalization of discrete latent variables mixed with continuous ones via sequential reduction, combined with automatic differentiation and the Laplace approximation, outperforming MCMC tools.
AI.motivation: Ecological and evolutionary models frequently contain mixed discrete and continuous latent variables, but fitting them with MCMC is prohibitively slow for large models.
AI.method: In the R package RTMB, small groups of related discrete variables are automatically sequentially reduced/marginalized, combined with automatic differentiation and the Laplace approximation to estimate parameters and predict both continuous and discrete variables.
AI.result: Benchmarked against JAGS and unmarked on occupancy, dynamic occupancy, N-mixture, and open dynamic N-mixture models. A multi-site open N-mixture model with a spatial latent variable (continuous Gaussian Markov random fields jointly estimated with discrete abundance dynamics) runs in under a minute. A phylogenetics case imputed a binary trait (viviparity), estimated its state-switching rates and effect on body size in female Liolaemus lizards.
AI.conclusion: Intuitive and efficient specification of mixed-type models enables more expressive representation of ecological and evolutionary dynamics, and phylogenetic comparative methods can estimate linkages among discrete and continuous traits.

title: GrassTop: Grassmannian k-mer Topology for Viral Classification and Phylogenetic Analysis
summary: We introduce GrassTop, a genome representation that integrates Grassmann manifolds and algebraic5 topology for viral classification and phylogenetic analysis. The framework begins by constructing mul-6 tiscale topological and spectral descriptors of (k)-mer positional patterns. It then extracts a low-rank7 subspace that summarizes variation across the filtration and compares genomes using a Grassmannian8 distance. Although the reported implementation uses the chordal distance, the framework is not re-9 stricted to this particular choice. We evaluate GrassTop on four families of viral classification datasets,10 four phylogenetic clustering datasets, and a sequence perturbation experiment. Under the reported 5-11 nearest-neighbor protocol, GrassTop achieves higher scores than five published alignment-free reference12 methods across all reported classification metrics and datasets. Its UPGMA (unweighted pair-group13 method using arithmetic averages) trees achieve an average label purity of 1.0 on every phylogenetic14 dataset. The perturbation experiment provides a more nuanced result: the subspace representation dif-15 fers most clearly from direct comparison of the unprojected feature matrices for SARS-CoV-2, whereas the16 differences are smaller or non-monotonic for the other datasets. Overall, these results support GrassTop17 as an effective topological-geometric representation for viral classification and phylogenetic analysis.

AI.tldr: GrassTop is a genome representation combining Grassmann manifolds and algebraic topology for viral classification and phylogenetics, outperforming five alignment-free methods.
AI.motivation: Viral classification and phylogenetic analysis need effective genome representations. The paper aims to provide a topological-geometric representation (GrassTop) that captures (k)-mer positional patterns and variation across filtrations, beyond existing alignment-free methods.
AI.method: GrassTop constructs multiscale topological and spectral descriptors of (k)-mer positional patterns, extracts a low-rank subspace summarizing variation across the filtration, and compares genomes via a Grassmannian distance (chordal distance used in implementation, but framework is general).
AI.result: On four viral classification families and four phylogenetic clustering datasets plus a perturbation experiment: under 5-NN, GrassTop scores higher than five published alignment-free methods across all classification metrics/datasets; UPGMA trees achieve average label purity of 1.0 on every phylogenetic dataset. Perturbation results are nuanced: subspace representation differs most clearly from unprojected feature matrices for SARS-CoV-2, smaller/non-monotonic differences for other datasets.
AI.conclusion: GrassTop is an effective topological-geometric representation for viral classification and phylogenetic analysis.

title: Speciation, extinction and explosions induced by sudden environmental changes
summary: We study the evolution of sexually reproducing populations subjected to sudden environmental changes. Using an individual based model we consider scenarios where abrupt changes can affect the carrying capacity, the mating range or the strength of assortativity, that controls the minimum similarity between individuals that allows mating to occur. We show that a boost in carrying capacity can either lead to new speciation events, thereby increasing biodiversity, or to widespread extinctions, causing the system to become dominated by a single species. A similar effect is observed with respect to the mating range. We show that the key factor determining the outcome of the process is genome length, i.e., the number of genes controlling reproduction and assortativity. We also show that when mating becomes more restrictive, increasing the degree of assortativity, a burst of speciation occurs. The explosion lasts only for a few generations, converging to values larger than before the change, but not as high as at the peak.

AI.tldr: An individual-based model shows that sudden environmental changes in sexually reproducing populations can trigger either speciation bursts or mass extinctions, with genome length as the key determinant.
AI.motivation: Populations face abrupt environmental changes, yet how such sudden shifts drive speciation versus extinction, and what factors control the outcome, remains unclear. This work investigates the mechanisms governing these divergent evolutionary outcomes.
AI.method: An individual-based model of sexually reproducing populations is used. Abrupt environmental changes are imposed affecting three factors: carrying capacity, mating range, and assortativity (minimum similarity required for mating).
AI.result: A boost in carrying capacity either causes new speciation events (raising biodiversity) or widespread extinctions dominated by a single species. Mating range shows similar effects. Genome length (number of genes controlling reproduction and assortativity) is the key factor. Increased assortativity triggers a speciation burst that lasts a few generations, settling above pre-change levels but below the peak.
AI.conclusion: The outcome of environmental change on speciation vs. extinction hinges on genome length. Restrictive mating promotes transient bursts of speciation that stabilize at moderately higher diversity.

title: Automated Volumetric Segmentation of Microaneurysms on OCT Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Purpose: To develop and validate a deep learning-based method for the automated identification and volumetric segmentation of microaneurysms (MAs) in diabetic retinopathy (DR) using OCT. Participants: A total of 125 participants were enrolled, including 20 healthy eyes, 27 with mild NPDR, 30 with moderate NPDR, 30 with severe NPDR, and 18 with PDR. Methods: We obtained multiple repeated 3x3-mm scans from each participant using a commercial 120-kHz spectral-domain OCT system (Solix; Visionix/Optovue, Inc., California, USA), which were registered and averaged to generate high-definition volumes. We developed a 3D deep learning network to segment MAs volumetrically. The input to the network consists of the original OCT volume concatenated with its reflectance-inverted counterpart. Expert graders manually delineated MAs to generate annotations. We evaluated model performance at multiple levels, including voxel-level segmentation, lesion-level detection, and eye-level diagnosis. Results: In the test dataset (20 healthy, 20 DR eyes), the algorithm demonstrated high voxel-level accuracy, with F1 scores of 79.2% on single volumes and 86.1% on averaged volumes. Lesion-level detection reached an F1 score of 96.0% (single) and 97.1% (averaged), while scan-level diagnostic accuracy for MA presence was 97.5% (single and averaged). Conclusions: A deep learning-based method can accurately identify and segment MAs volumetrically on OCT, enabling quantification and characterization, and potentially aiding in the diagnosis, monitoring, and management of DR.

AI.tldr: A 3D deep learning network segments microaneurysms volumetrically on OCT, achieving high voxel, lesion, and eye-level performance for diabetic retinopathy assessment.
AI.motivation: Automated identification and volumetric segmentation of microaneurysms (MAs) in diabetic retinopathy (DR) using OCT is needed to enable quantification and characterization, potentially aiding diagnosis, monitoring, and management of DR.
AI.method: 125 participants (20 healthy, 27 mild NPDR, 30 moderate NPDR, 30 severe NPDR, 18 PDR) underwent repeated 3x3-mm scans with a 120-kHz spectral-domain OCT system, registered and averaged into high-definition volumes. A 3D deep learning network segmented MAs volumetrically; input was the original OCT volume concatenated with its reflectance-inverted counterpart. Expert graders manually delineated MAs for annotation. Performance was evaluated at voxel, lesion, and eye levels.
AI.result: On the test dataset (20 healthy, 20 DR eyes), voxel-level F1 was 79.2% (single volumes) and 86.1% (averaged volumes); lesion-level detection F1 was 96.0% (single) and 97.1% (averaged); scan-level diagnostic accuracy for MA presence was 97.5% for both single and averaged volumes.
AI.conclusion: A deep learning-based method can accurately identify and segment MAs volumetrically on OCT, enabling quantification and characterization, and potentially aiding in the diagnosis, monitoring, and management of DR.

title: Structures of the Basic Reproduction Number $R_0$ Across Compartmental Disease Models
summary: The basic reproduction number $R_0$ is the central dimensionless quantity in mathematical epidemiology, characterizing the threshold for disease outbreak and the early growth rate of an epidemic. The algebraic form of $R_0$ varies widely across models of distinct transmission mechanisms, and its interpretation can yield further biological insight into transmission dynamics and disease intervention. We present a structural taxonomy of $R_0$ for compartmental ordinary differential equation models spanning a range of disease transmission features, including staged progression, differential infectivity, competing strains, vector-borne transmission, sexually transmitted infection, recurrent infection, maternal transmission, and gene drive inheritance. For each structural class, we provide a worked example, deriving $R_0$ via the next-generation matrix approach and interpreting the resulting algebraic expression in terms of the underlying transmission pathway. By unifying disparate derivations under a single structural framework, we clarify when and why particular algebraic forms of $R_0$ arise. This review serves both as a research synthesis and as a self-contained pedagogical reference for students and researchers entering the field.

AI.tldr: This review presents a structural taxonomy of the basic reproduction number $R_0$ for compartmental ODE epidemic models, organizing diverse transmission mechanisms under a unified next-generation-matrix framework with worked examples and interpretations.
AI.motivation: The algebraic form of $R_0$ varies widely across models of distinct transmission mechanisms, and there is a need to clarify when and why particular algebraic forms arise. A unified structural perspective can yield biological insight into transmission dynamics and disease intervention.
AI.method: The authors construct a structural taxonomy of $R_0$ for compartmental ordinary differential equation models, covering features such as staged progression, differential infectivity, competing strains, vector-borne transmission, sexually transmitted infection, recurrent infection, maternal transmission, and gene drive inheritance. For each structural class, they derive $R_0$ via the next-generation matrix approach and interpret the resulting algebraic expressions in terms of underlying transmission pathways.
AI.result: The paper provides worked examples for each structural class, unifying disparate derivations under a single structural framework and clarifying the conditions under which particular algebraic forms of $R_0$ emerge.
AI.conclusion: The review serves as both a research synthesis and a self-contained pedagogical reference for students and researchers entering the field of mathematical epidemiology.

title: Hierarchical emergence of network bursting in a four-cell central pattern generator model
summary: How can a neural circuit rhythmically burst when none of its constituent neurons can endogenously do so? We address this question through a bottom-up reconstruction of a 4-cell neural circuit modeled after the swim central pattern generator (CPG) of the sea slug \textit{Dendronotus iris}. We first map the intrinsic regimes of a swim interneuron (SiN) model neuron and show that slow mutual inhibition can generate anti-phase bursting in a half-center oscillator (HCO) assembled from tonic-spiking or quiescent cells. A slow--fast phase-space deconstruction explains this pairwise rhythm as a release mechanism. We then move on to CPG parametrization, in which cells 1 and 2 are quiescent, while cells 3 and 4 are tonic spikers but their isolated HCO can only exhibit tonic spiking or suppression. Bursting therefore does not arise at either the cellular or HCO level. It appears only after the two modules are assembled into the complete 4-cell network, where cross excitation, cross inhibition, and rectified electrical coupling act together to support a robust network rhythm-generation. Event-based symbolic encoding and GPU-parallel parameter sweeps show that this higher-order collective state occupies extended parameter domains rather than a single tuned point, and they quantify how the network interactions reshape those domains and the spike counts per burst. Symbolic sweeps identify the healthy range of activity regimes (periodic sequences) and transition boundaries; Lempel--Ziv complexity is used as a descriptor of aperiodic symbolic output rather than as proof of chaos or dynamical instability. Our results establish a hierarchy of rhythm generation---from intrinsic cell dynamics, through conditional HCO bursting, to bursting that emerges only in the fully assembled 4-cell CPG---and provide experimentally accessible predictions for perturbing its chemical and electrical couplings.

AI.tldr: A 4-cell model of the Dendronotus swim CPG shows rhythmic bursting that exists at no lower level: not in single cells, and not in isolated half-center oscillators, but only when the full network is assembled.
AI.motivation: The paper asks how a neural circuit can burst rhythmically when none of its constituent neurons can endogenously burst. This questions the origin of network-level rhythm generation.
AI.method: Bottom-up reconstruction of a 4-cell circuit modeled on the sea slug swim CPG. Mapping of intrinsic SiN regimes; slow-fast phase-space deconstruction; CPG parametrization with two quiescent and two tonic-spiking cells; event-based symbolic encoding and GPU-parallel parameter sweeps; Lempel-Ziv complexity as a descriptor of aperiodic output.
AI.result: Slow mutual inhibition produces anti-phase bursting in an HCO of tonic or quiescent cells via a release mechanism. In the 4-cell CPG, bursting appears only when cross excitation, cross inhibition, and rectified electrical coupling act together. This collective state occupies extended parameter domains, with symbolic sweeps identifying healthy periodic regimes and transition boundaries.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a hierarchy of rhythm generation: intrinsic cell dynamics, conditional HCO bursting, and bursting emerging only in the fully assembled 4-cell CPG. They provide experimentally testable predictions for perturbing chemical and electrical couplings.

title: URCHIN: A Horizontal Spiking Language Model for Data-Constrained Pretraining
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to the BabyLM Challenge 2026 (BabyLM Workshop, EMNLP 2026)
summary: The BabyLM challenge measures how much language a model can learn from developmentally-plausible, child-scale data rather than internet-scale corpora, yet prior language models forgo the biological constraints of the neural circuitry that acquires human language: spiking neurons separated into excitatory and inhibitory populations wired by a recurrent lateral connectome. This paper presents URCHIN (Unified Recurrent Connectome with Horizontal Integrate-and-fire Neurons), which applies the Parallelized Hierarchical Connectome Spiking State-space Model (PHCSSM) to language modeling: leaky integrate-and-fire neurons coupled by a Dale's-law lateral connectome resolve each token through a multi-transmission loop that recirculates activity to a fixed point. The instantiation is deliberately minimal: a single horizontal layer of 128 neurons, no attention, and 4.23M parameters. Two implementations share one set of weights and produce identical benchmark scores, so URCHIN is trained once and deployed either way with no conversion step: a parallel state-space model (SSM) scan that is GPU-efficient for training, or an event-driven recurrent spiking neural network (RSNN) with constant-cost inference for CPU or neuromorphic edge deployment. Across all three BabyLM tracks (Strict-100M, Strict-Small, and Multilingual), URCHIN offers a biologically plausible, efficient, and directly deployable reference point.

AI.tldr: URCHIN is a bio-plausible spiking language model for BabyLM: a single 128-neuron lateral layer of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with Dale's-law E/I connectivity, trained as a parallel SSM and deployable as an event-driven RSNN with constant-cost inference.
AI.motivation: BabyLM tests how much language a model can learn from child-scale data, but prior models ignore the biological constraints of human language circuitry: spiking neurons split into excitatory and inhibitory populations wired by a recurrent lateral connectome.
AI.method: Applies the Parallelized Hierarchical Connectome Spiking State-space Model (PHCSSM). Leaky integrate-and-fire neurons coupled by a Dale's-law lateral connectome resolve each token via a multi-transmission loop recirculating activity to a fixed point. Deliberately minimal: one horizontal layer of 128 neurons, no attention, 4.23M params. One weight set supports two implementations with identical scores and no conversion: a GPU-efficient parallel SSM scan for training, or an event-driven RSNN with constant-cost inference for CPU/neuromorphic edge.
AI.result: Both implementations share weights and produce identical benchmark scores. Evaluated across all three BabyLM tracks: Strict-100M, Strict-Small, and Multilingual.
AI.conclusion: URCHIN provides a biologically plausible, efficient, and directly deployable reference point for BabyLM without conversion between training and deployment.

title: Fragmented uptake drives lipid accumulation in macrophage cannibalistic efferocytosis
summary: Efferocytosis, the clearance of dying cells typically by macrophages, is essential for tissue homeostasis and the resolution of inflammation. Previous experiments by Ford et al. (Proc. R. Soc. B, 2019) showed that cannibalistic efferocytosis redistributes endogenous lipid from dying macrophages into the surviving population, but existing mathematical models do not reproduce the observed population dynamics and lipid distributions. Here, fifteen candidate models are compared, combining three mechanisms of apoptotic material uptake with five forms of the macrophage death rate. Model comparison is guided by the Akaike Information Criterion and qualitative agreement with the observed lipid distributions. Numerical solutions show that whole-cell uptake models predict internal maxima that are absent from the data, whereas nibbling uptake produces distributions that are too concentrated about their means. By contrast, intermediate "fragmented" uptake models provide substantially improved agreement when combined with either linear lipid-dependent or exponential time-dependent death rates. The fitted models predict that smaller fragments from dying cells are ingested at higher frequency than larger ones. This analysis provides new insight into how efferocytosis shapes the distribution of lipid within macrophage populations and highlights the importance of distribution-level data for distinguishing between mechanistic models that reproduce similar population-average dynamics.

AI.tldr: Fifteen candidate models of efferocytosis are compared to reproduce macrophage population dynamics and lipid distributions, with "fragmented" uptake combined with linear lipid-dependent or exponential time-dependent death rates providing the best fit.
AI.motivation: Efferocytosis is essential for tissue homeostasis and inflammation resolution. Prior experiments (Ford et al., 2019) showed cannibalistic efferocytosis redistributes endogenous lipid from dying to surviving macrophages, but existing mathematical models fail to reproduce the observed population dynamics and lipid distributions, prompting a systematic model comparison.
AI.method: Fifteen candidate models were compared, combining three mechanisms of apoptotic material uptake (whole-cell, nibbling, fragmented) with five forms of the macrophage death rate. Model comparison used the Akaike Information Criterion and qualitative agreement with observed lipid distributions.
AI.result: Whole-cell uptake models predict internal maxima absent from the data, while nibbling uptake produces distributions too concentrated around their means. Intermediate "fragmented" uptake models agree substantially better, especially when combined with linear lipid-dependent or exponential time-dependent death rates. Fitted models predict smaller fragments are ingested more frequently than larger ones.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides new insight into how efferocytosis shapes lipid distribution within macrophage populations and highlights the importance of distribution-level data for distinguishing mechanistic models that reproduce similar population-average dynamics.

title: RAGCell: Retrieval-Augmented Generation as Supervision for Versatile Single-cell Analysis
summary:
Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are transforming computational biology by enabling generalizable, task-agnostic representations for versatile single-cell analysis. Despite their progress in facilitating rapid deployment for downstream tasks, off-the-shelf scFMs still have some overlooked concerns: (I) (Pretraining Cost.) Pretrain-based scFMs necessitate pretraining on a vast volume of cells, rendering it draining resources in applications. (II) (Heterogeneous Gap.) Large Language Models (LLM)-based scFMs ignore the tremendous heterogeneous gap between LLM textual and raw cellular spaces, leading to insufficient capability when facing downstream tasks.
  To this end, we introduce RAGCell, a versatile single-cell analysis framework that achieves a double-win in both cost-effectiveness and high performance. The success of RAGCell lies in two key aspects: Leveraging LLMs to construct cell-level and feature-level knowledge databases, which serve as supervision signals for training the cell model and significantly reduce the training cost ($>$pretrain-based scFMs). Aligning cell representations with text embeddings from the bi-level knowledge databases, enabling knowledge transfer from textual spaces to cellular spaces and effectively mitigating the heterogeneous gap ($>$LLM-based scFMs). Through extensive experiments on six downstream single-cell analysis tasks, we demonstrate that RAGCell achieves outstanding performance compared to state-of-the-art scFMs while operating at less than $\sim$1/10 the cost of pretrain-based scFMs.

AI.tldr: RAGCell is a single-cell analysis framework using retrieval-augmented knowledge databases built by LLMs to achieve cost-effective and high-performance single-cell analysis, outperforming pretrain-based and LLM-based scFMs at ~1/10 the cost.
AI.motivation: Off-the-shelf single-cell foundation models (scFMs) have two overlooked issues: (I) Pretraining Cost—pretrain-based scFMs require vast cell volumes, draining resources; (II) Heterogeneous Gap—LLM-based scFMs ignore the heterogeneous gap between LLM textual and raw cellular spaces, limiting downstream performance.
AI.method: RAGCell leverages LLMs to construct cell-level and feature-level knowledge databases that serve as supervision signals for training the cell model, reducing training cost. It aligns cell representations with text embeddings from these bi-level knowledge databases, transferring knowledge from textual to cellular spaces and mitigating the heterogeneous gap.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six downstream single-cell analysis tasks show RAGCell achieves outstanding performance compared to state-of-the-art scFMs while operating at less than ~1/10 the cost of pretrain-based scFMs.
AI.conclusion: RAGCell delivers a double-win in cost-effectiveness and high performance, offering a versatile single-cell analysis framework superior to both pretrain-based and LLM-based scFMs.

title: Nonlinear dynamics of random neural networks with second-order synaptic motifs
summary: Classical theories of random neural networks typically assume independent connectivity, overlooking the local motif structures prevalent in biological circuits. Here, we investigate how four second-order synaptic motifs (chain, reciprocal, convergent, and divergent) shape the dynamics of nonlinear firing-rate networks. While previous studies have established that chain correlations generate outlier eigenvalues, we demonstrate that these motifs also jointly reshape the Jacobian eigenvalue bulk. Using the path-integral formalism, we derive a dynamic mean-field theory which reveals that the chain motif acts as a retarded feedback of the ensemble-mean activity through the response kernel, producing a rich repertoire of dynamical regimes, including ferromagnetic states and limit cycles. At sufficiently large magnitude, negative chain correlations produce a glassy, multistable regime that was previously mainly associated with partially symmetric networks. Our theory also distinguishes convergent from divergent motifs: divergent correlations primarily rescale temporal noise, while convergent correlations suppress temporal chaos by converting nonzero mean activity into quenched heterogeneity. Finally, analyses of the Lyapunov spectrum and participation-ratio dimension show that motif structure changes the geometry of chaotic activity, reducing entropy production and attractor dimensionality even when the effective spectral edge is held fixed. Together, these findings establish second-order motifs as a fundamental structural mechanism governing the dynamical regimes of local cortical circuits.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a dynamic mean-field theory for nonlinear firing-rate networks that incorporates four second-order synaptic motifs (chain, reciprocal, convergent, divergent), showing how these local structures reshape Jacobian spectra and produce diverse dynamical regimes beyond classical independent-connectivity models.
AI.motivation: Classical random neural network theories assume independent connectivity and ignore local motif structures common in biological circuits, limiting their ability to capture realistic cortical dynamics.
AI.method: The authors use path-integral formalism to derive a dynamic mean-field theory for nonlinear firing-rate networks with four second-order motifs, and analyze the Jacobian eigenvalue bulk, Lyapunov spectrum, and participation-ratio dimension.
AI.result: Chain motifs generate outlier eigenvalues and act as retarded feedback via the response kernel, producing ferromagnetic states and limit cycles; strong negative chain correlations yield a glassy multistable regime. Divergent motifs rescale temporal noise, while convergent motifs suppress chaos by converting mean activity into quenched heterogeneity. Motif structure reduces entropy production and attractor dimensionality even at fixed spectral edge.
AI.conclusion: Second-order motifs are a fundamental structural mechanism governing the dynamical regimes and geometry of chaotic activity in local cortical circuits.

title: MIRAGE: Measuring Interpolation and Redundancy in Affinity GEneralization
summary: Deep learning now underpins structure-based drug design, from complex and affinity prediction to ligand ranking and pose generation. Recent co-folding models reportedly approach free-energy-perturbation accuracy at far lower cost. Yet standard evaluation, a single held-out correlation or pooled pose-success rate, cannot separate transferable binding principles from repeated exposure to related protein families in public databases, and practical success depends on genuinely novel targets. We introduce MIRAGE (Measuring Interpolation and Redundancy in Affinity GEneralization), a plug-in benchmark treating historical public family support (through 2019) as an explicit variable, applying a family-support axis to affinity and pose prediction via matched strata, family-disjoint controls, ligand-only baselines, and temporal evaluation. Co-folder affinity accuracy rises sharply with family support, while shallow controls that cannot exploit the test family stay flat, large for co-folders and near zero for every family-disjoint or trivial control. For Nesso-1 it survives covariate, conditioning, balancing, and clustering checks; Boltz-2's endpoint is limited by coverage. It localizes to family support rather than ligand chemistry, approaching a level from family identity alone. Rankings reverse on novel families, where a family-disjoint random forest leads both co-folders, significantly vs Nesso-1. On one external low-support target, neither co-folder beats molecular weight, corroborative rather than population-level evidence. gnina shows significant support dependence in rescoring whereas smina does not; MSA-free pose engines show larger gaps than smina redocking. This redundancy-driven inflation differs from conventional leakage. We propose reporting performance across family support plus excess over a support-insensitive baseline, and release MIRAGE as an installable benchmark and dataset.

AI.tldr: MIRAGE benchmarks protein-family support as an explicit variable, revealing co-folding drug-design models' affinity/pose gains largely reflect redundancy with public training families, not generalizable binding principles.
AI.motivation: Standard single held-out correlation or pooled pose-success metrics cannot separate transferable binding principles from repeated exposure to related protein families in public databases, yet practical success depends on genuinely novel targets.
AI.method: MIRAGE (Measuring Interpolation and Redundancy in Affinity GEneralization) is a plug-in benchmark treating historical public family support (through 2019) as an explicit variable, using a family-support axis via matched strata, family-disjoint controls, ligand-only baselines, and temporal evaluation for affinity and pose prediction.
AI.result: Co-folder affinity accuracy rises sharply with family support while shallow controls stay flat; large for co-folders, near zero for family-disjoint/trivial controls. Nesso-1 survives covariate, conditioning, balancing, and clustering checks; Boltz-2's endpoint is limited by coverage. Effects localize to family support, not ligand chemistry. Rankings reverse on novel families (family-disjoint random forest leads both co-folders). On one external low-support target, neither co-folder beats molecular weight. gnina shows significant support dependence in rescoring; smina does not.
AI.conclusion: The redundancy-driven inflation differs from conventional leakage. Recommend reporting performance across family support plus excess over a support-insensitive baseline. MIRAGE released as an installable benchmark and dataset.

title: How deterministic trajectories and their fluctuations underlie allele-frequency statistics in the strong-selection regime
summary:
In many biological contexts selection is strong relative to genetic drift. Working under the diffusion approximation, we define $R = 2N_{e}|s|$, where $N_{e}$ is the effective population size and $s$ is the selection coefficient associated with a focal allele. Strong selection corresponds to $R \gg1$ and can occur for relatively modest parameter values. For example, $N_e = 10^3$ and $s = 10^{-2}$ yield $R = 20$. The focus of this work is on statistics of the allele frequency distribution in the strong selection regime. In this regime, standard approximations often break down. For instance, under strong positive selection ($R\gg1$ and $s>0$), trajectories that proceed to fixation seem to dominate allele frequency statistics. However, omission of trajectories that ultimately achieve loss can lead to large errors.
  Over timescales where mutation can be neglected, all allele frequency trajectories fall into one of two classes: those that eventually achieve fixation and those that eventually achieve loss. We ensure that both types of trajectory contribute to time-dependent statistics, by separately conditioning on the eventual fixation and eventual loss of the focal allele. For large $R$, we determine approximations for allele-frequency statistics under a small noise approximation that derives contributions from two deterministic trajectories, one achieving fixation the other loss, along with fluctuations around these two trajectories. Such an approach yields the correct long time values of the mean allele frequency and its variance. Numerical comparisons with the Wright-Fisher model indicate that the contribution of the deterministic trajectories alone, to a statistic, may not always be sufficient for good accuracy, but with the inclusion of fluctuations, reasonable accuracy is obtained.

AI.tldr: This paper develops approximations for allele frequency statistics under strong selection (R = 2Ne|s| >> 1) using a small-noise expansion around two deterministic trajectories—one conditioned on eventual fixation and one on eventual loss—including fluctuations around each.
AI.motivation: Standard diffusion approximations break down in the strong selection regime. In particular, focusing only on trajectories leading to fixation (ignoring those that achieve loss) can cause large errors, so both outcome classes must be accounted for.
AI.method: Working under the diffusion approximation, the authors condition separately on eventual fixation and eventual loss over timescales where mutation is negligible. For large R, they use a small-noise approximation combining contributions from two deterministic trajectories (fixation and loss) plus fluctuations around them.
AI.result: The approach recovers correct long-time values of the mean allele frequency and its variance. Numerical comparisons with the Wright-Fisher model show that deterministic trajectories alone are not always accurate, but including fluctuations yields reasonable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for both fixation- and loss-bound trajectories with fluctuation corrections gives accurate allele frequency statistics in the strong selection regime, where standard approximations fail.

title: Evolution of Fast and Slow Life Histories in Resource-Constrained Populations with Mass-Mortality Events
summary:
We study the evolution of the speed of life history in populations competing for a single growth-limiting resource subject to demographic stochasticity and mass mortality events. We focus on a quasi-neutral regime in which competing types have equal resource-use efficiency but differ in life-history speed.
  In the large-carrying-capacity scaling limit, we reduce the model to a one-dimensional jump-diffusion supported on the manifold of ecological equilibria. The drift and diffusion components capture the joint effects of demographic stochasticity and density regulation, while the jump component is driven by the catastrophic mortality events. Using this limiting process, we derive a first-order approximation for the fixation probability of an invading type that differs slightly in life history speed from the resident population. Calculations show that small demographic events tend to favor slower life histories, whereas catastrophic mortality events create transient periods of resource abundance that benefit faster types. The interaction of these two evolutionary forces allows for the existence of a nontrivial evolutionarily attractive life-history speed, which is an increasing function of the frequency and intensity of the catastrophic mortality events.
  These results provide a rigorous mathematical framework for some classical r/K-selection arguments, and furthermore demonstrate how mass mortality events can maintain selection for faster life histories even in resource-constrained populations.

AI.tldr: The paper models the evolution of life-history speed in competing populations under demographic stochasticity and mass mortality events, showing a nontrivial evolutionarily attractive speed that increases with catastrophe frequency and intensity.
AI.motivation: Classical r/K-selection arguments lack rigorous mathematical grounding, especially regarding how stochastic demographic events and catastrophic mortality jointly shape selection on life-history speed in resource-constrained populations.
AI.method: Focusing on a quasi-neutral regime (equal resource-use efficiency, differing life-history speed), the authors take a large-carrying-capacity scaling limit to reduce the model to a one-dimensional jump-diffusion process on the manifold of ecological equilibria. Drift and diffusion capture demographic stochasticity and density regulation; jumps capture mass mortality. They derive a first-order approximation of the fixation probability for a slightly different invading type.
AI.result: Small demographic events favor slower life histories, while catastrophic mortality events create transient resource abundance benefiting faster types. Their interaction yields a nontrivial evolutionarily attractive life-history speed that increases with catastrophe frequency and intensity.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rigorous framework for classical r/K-selection arguments and shows that mass mortality events can sustain selection for faster life histories even in resource-constrained populations.

title: Telegraph Processes with Extrinsic Fluctuations: Burst Dynamics and an Application to Domestic Cat Activity
summary: Animal activity often consists of intermittent bursts separated by prolonged periods of inactivity. Here, we describe this behavior using a two-state telegraph process with extrinsically fluctuating transition rates. We derived analytical expressions for the stationary behavior of the system and characterized how stationary fluctuations in the effective transition rates modified the activity and residence time statistics. In particular, we show that whereas fixed transition rates lead to exponential residence-time distributions, stationary rate fluctuations generate effective Lomax distributions with heavier tails. We also found that fluctuations can either increase or decrease the mean occupancy of the active state, and that when the fluctuations in the two transition rates are equal, their effect on the stationary occupancy becomes indistinguishable from the case without fluctuations. We assessed the parameter inference using synthetic data and applied the framework to observations of a domestic cat. For synthetic data, accounting for extrinsic fluctuations substantially improved the recovery of the kinetic parameters used to generate the data. In the experimental data, the inferred variability of the inactive-to-active transition rate was substantially larger than that of the active-to-inactive rate. These results establish a tractable framework for studying stochastic switching systems in which extrinsic variability reshapes burst and residence-time statistics.

AI.tldr: This paper models intermittent animal activity as a two-state telegraph process with extrinsically fluctuating transition rates, deriving analytical statistics and showing that rate fluctuations generate Lomax (heavier-tailed) residence-time distributions.
AI.motivation: Animal activity consists of intermittent bursts separated by prolonged inactivity, and existing fixed-rate models may not capture how extrinsic variability reshapes activity and residence-time statistics.
AI.method: A two-state telegraph process with extrinsically fluctuating transition rates is analyzed analytically for stationary behavior. Parameter inference was assessed on synthetic data and then applied to observations of a domestic cat.
AI.result: Fixed rates yield exponential residence-time distributions, while stationary rate fluctuations produce effective Lomax distributions with heavier tails. Fluctuations can increase or decrease mean active-state occupancy, and equal fluctuations in both rates make occupancy indistinguishable from the no-fluctuation case. Inference on synthetic data improved kinetic parameter recovery when accounting for extrinsic fluctuations; in cat data, inactive-to-active rate variability exceeded active-to-inactive variability.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a tractable approach for studying stochastic switching systems where extrinsic variability reshapes burst and residence-time statistics.

title: TractSpLearn: Specialized Shared-Manifold Learning for Individualized Detection of Subtle White Matter Alterations in Mild Traumatic Brain Injury
comment: Ali Al-Husseini and Yi Chen contributed equally as second authors. Niklas Marklund, Christophe Phillips and Evgenios N. Kornaropoulos contributed equally as last authors
summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) often leads to subtle white matter damage that remains undetected on conventional MRI. Diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), an extension of diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), provides complementary information on non-Gaussian water diffusion and is sensitive to complex white-matter microstructure. With the advent of ultra-high-field MRI, the spatial resolution and signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) have been significantly enhanced, enabling more precise visualization of subtle abnormalities. Building on these advances, we developed TractSpLearn, an individualized tract-based learning framework that jointly considers within-group variability and between-group differences. Unlike the original TractLearn framework, which learns a normative manifold exclusively from healthy controls, TractSpLearn incorporates both healthy controls and patients to learn a shared manifold with a healthy-anchored representation and an additional patient-related component. To assess the performance of the proposed method, we compared TractSpLearn with the original TractLearn in three cohorts: (i) healthy controls (HC), (ii) athletes with persistent post-concussive syndromes (PPCS), and (iii) athletes with repeated head injuries (RHI), with abnormalities particularly evident in axial kurtosis (AK) and mean diffusivity (MD). In RHI, TractSpLearn highlighted recurrent abnormalities across patients. In the PPCS cohort, the overall group-level differences were more modest, potentially reflecting both limited statistical power due to the small sample size and partial normalization of white-matter alterations during recovery. Still TractSpLearn identified abnormality evidence in more patients and across more affected tracts than TractLearn.

AI.tldr: TractSpLearn is an individualized tract-based learning framework using ultra-high-field DKI that jointly models within-group variability and between-group differences to detect subtle white-matter abnormalities after TBI, outperforming TractLearn.
AI.motivation: TBI often causes subtle white-matter damage undetected by conventional MRI. Existing tract-based methods like TractLearn learn a normative manifold only from healthy controls, ignoring patient-related variability and potentially missing individualized abnormalities.
AI.method: Leveraging ultra-high-field MRI DKI data, the authors propose TractSpLearn, which incorporates both healthy controls and patients to learn a shared manifold with a healthy-anchored representation plus a patient-related component, capturing within-group variability and between-group differences. It was compared with TractLearn across HC, PPCS, and RHI cohorts using AK and MD metrics.
AI.result: In the RHI cohort, TractSpLearn highlighted recurrent abnormalities across patients. In the PPCS cohort, group-level differences were modest (possibly due to small sample size and partial normalization during recovery), yet TractSpLearn identified abnormalities in more patients and more affected tracts than TractLearn.
AI.conclusion: TractSpLearn improves sensitivity for detecting subtle white-matter abnormalities in TBI by jointly modeling healthy and patient data, offering an individualized approach superior to control-only normative frameworks.

title: Synthesizing State-of-the-Art Structure Predictions from Soup of Co-folding Models
summary: Co-folding models have advanced rapidly, yet no single model consistently performs best across all biomolecular complexes. This raises the question of whether independently trained co-folding models encode complementary information that can be transferred across co-folding models. We introduce SoupFold, which improves co-folding predictions by learning simple mappings between the representation spaces of co-folding models. At inference time, SoupFold transfers and incorporates representations from other co-folding models to update the representation used for structure prediction. Importantly, this does not re-train the co-folding models. We evaluate SoupFold on protein-protein and protein-ligand prediction tasks of FoldBench using AlphaFold3, Protenix, ESMFold2, and OpenDDE. By combining their representations, SoupFold achieves state-of-the-art performance on both protein-protein and protein-ligand structure prediction, showing that independently trained co-folding models encode complementary information that can be effectively transferred across models.

AI.tldr: SoupFold improves co-folding structure prediction by learning simple mappings to transfer representations between independently trained co-folding models without retraining them.
AI.motivation: No single co-folding model consistently performs best across all biomolecular complexes, prompting the question of whether independently trained models encode complementary information that can be transferred across models.
AI.method: SoupFold learns simple mappings between the representation spaces of different co-folding models. At inference, it transfers and incorporates representations from other models to update the prediction representation, without retraining any co-folding model.
AI.result: Evaluated on protein-protein and protein-ligand tasks of FoldBench using AlphaFold3, Protenix, ESMFold2, and OpenDDE, SoupFold achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks.
AI.conclusion: Independently trained co-folding models encode complementary information that can be effectively transferred across models, improving structure prediction.

title: Multiscale modeling of host-pathogen interactions and mucociliary clearance during non-tuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary infection
summary:
Non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infections are a clinical challenge in cystic fibrosis (CF), where impaired mucociliary clearance and altered mucus rheology promote bacterial colonization despite host immune responses. Understanding how bacterial growth, immune cell dynamics, and mucus transport regulate infection progression is difficult because these processes interact across spatial and temporal scales. We develop a computational framework bridging a mechanistic agent-based model (ABM) of NTM infection with a spatially resolved partial differential equation (PDE) model. The PDE model couples bacterial proliferation, macrophage chemotaxis, immune-mediated clearance, mucus degradation, and viscoelastic transport in a two-compartment geometry representing mucus and lung tissue. Parameters are calibrated using data from the established ABM, yielding an efficient continuum representation while preserving cellular mechanisms.
  The PDE model reproduces bacterial and macrophage dynamics and enables analyses of mucus-related mechanisms and therapies. Sensitivity analysis identifies mucus viscosity, bacterial diffusivity, and macrophage mobility as key regulators of bacterial persistence through mucociliary clearance and tissue colonization. Simulations reveal nonlinear effects of mucolytic therapies: enhanced clearance reduces bacterial burden in mucus, whereas excessive viscosity reduction may promote migration into lung tissue, supporting combination with antibacterial treatment. This framework provides a quantitative platform for studying pulmonary infections, evaluating therapies, and developing patient-specific digital twins.

AI.tldr: A PDE-based continuum model of NTM infection in cystic fibrosis, calibrated from an agent-based model, reveals mucus viscosity, bacterial diffusivity, and macrophage mobility as key regulators and shows that excessive mucolytic therapy may worsen tissue colonization.
AI.motivation: NTM infections are challenging in cystic fibrosis because impaired mucociliary clearance and altered mucus rheology drive colonization despite immune responses. Understanding how bacterial growth, immune dynamics, and mucus transport interact across spatial and temporal scales is difficult, motivating a computational framework that bridges cellular and continuum descriptions.
AI.method: The authors build a spatially resolved PDE model coupled to a mechanistic agent-based model (ABM). The PDE couples bacterial proliferation, macrophage chemotaxis, immune-mediated clearance, mucus degradation, and viscoelastic transport in a two-compartment geometry representing mucus and lung tissue. Parameters are calibrated using data from the established ABM.
AI.result: The PDE model reproduces bacterial and macrophage dynamics. Sensitivity analysis identifies mucus viscosity, bacterial diffusivity, and macrophage mobility as key regulators of bacterial persistence via mucociliary clearance and tissue colonization. Simulations show nonlinear mucolytic therapy effects: enhanced clearance lowers bacterial burden in mucus, but excessive viscosity reduction may promote migration into lung tissue.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a quantitative platform for studying pulmonary infections, evaluating therapies, and developing patient-specific digital twins, suggesting mucolytic therapy should be combined with antibacterial treatment.

title: When Teachers Smile or Frown: A Profile-Based Analysis of Achievement Emotions
summary: Achievement emotions shape how students engage with and learn from academic tasks, yet most studies examine individual emotions rather than co-occurring affective profiles and their dynamics. We examined latent achievement-emotion profiles and their transitions following exposure to different instructor facial expressions during a video lecture. Self-reported data from 78 Grade VII and VIII students revealed three profiles: enthusiastic, demotivated, and vulnerable. Profile transitions differed across instructor conditions, with happy expressions favouring more adaptive transitions and angry expressions favouring transitions toward demotivation. Exploratory factor analysis and Bayesian structural modelling further identified preparedness and cognitive restraint as regulatory dimensions associated with profile switching.

AI.tldr: The study identifies three latent achievement-emotion profiles (enthusiastic, demotivated, vulnerable) in 78 middle-school students and shows their transitions depend on instructor facial expressions during video lectures.
AI.motivation: Most research examines individual achievement emotions separately, overlooking how multiple emotions co-occur as affective profiles and how these profiles change. Understanding profile dynamics and instructor-driven influences can better explain student engagement and learning.
AI.method: 78 Grade VII-VIII students watched a video lecture under different instructor facial-expression conditions. Latent profile analysis identified emotion profiles; transitions were compared across conditions. Exploratory factor analysis and Bayesian structural modelling examined regulatory dimensions (preparedness, cognitive restraint) linked to profile switching.
AI.result: Three profiles emerged: enthusiastic, demotivated, and vulnerable. Transitions varied by instructor condition—happy expressions promoted adaptive transitions, while angry expressions pushed students toward demotivation. Preparedness and cognitive restraint were associated with profile switching.
AI.conclusion: Instructor facial expressions shape students' co-occurring achievement-emotion profiles and their transitions. Regulatory factors like preparedness and cognitive restraint may moderate these shifts, suggesting implications for instructional affect and emotion regulation in learning.

title: Mutual Information in Coupled Double Quantum Dots: A Simple Analytic Model for Potential Artificial Consciousness
summary: The integrated information theory is thought to be a key clue towards the theoretical understanding of consciousness. In this study, we propose a simple numerical model comprising a set of coupled double quantum dots, where the disconnection of the elements is represented by the removal of Coulomb interaction between the quantum dots, for the quantitative investigation of integrated information. As a measure of integrated information, we calculate the mutual information in the model system, as the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the connected and disconnected status, through the probability distribution of the electronic states from the master transition-rate equations. We reasonably demonstrate that the increase in the strength of interaction between the quantum dots leads to higher mutual information, owing to the larger divergence in the probability distributions of the electronic states. Our model setup could be a useful basic tool for numerical analyses in the field of integrated information theory.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a coupled double quantum dot model to numerically quantify integrated information, showing that stronger Coulomb interaction increases mutual information.
AI.motivation: Integrated information theory is considered a key clue to theoretically understanding consciousness, and a quantitative numerical framework is needed to investigate integrated information.
AI.method: A simple numerical model of coupled double quantum dots is introduced, where element disconnection corresponds to removing Coulomb interaction. Mutual information is computed as the Kullback-Leibler divergence between connected and disconnected states, using electronic state probability distributions derived from master transition-rate equations.
AI.result: Stronger interaction between quantum dots leads to higher mutual information, due to larger divergence in the probability distributions of electronic states.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model setup could serve as a useful basic tool for numerical analyses in integrated information theory.

title: A Stochastic Model of Intracellular Calcium Concentrations
summary: In this paper, we study a slow-fast model of Intracellular Calcium Concentrations (ICC) within a stochastic framework, where stochastic perturbations are introduced to capture the intrinsic randomness of such biological systems. We first analyse the three-dimensional single-cell model, based on the FitzHugh-Nagumo structure, and subsequently extend the analysis to a coupled two-cell six-dimensional setting. We prove existence and uniqueness of solutions and establish positivity of the calcium variable. We obtain explicit mean-square stability estimates around deterministic equilibria and quantify how they depend on the noise intensity. Numerical simulations for both the single-cell and coupled systems illustrate relevant qualitative behaviours and reveal additional dynamical features arising in the stochastic framework.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a stochastic slow-fast model of intracellular calcium concentrations (ICC), proving solution existence/uniqueness, positivity, and mean-square stability for both single-cell (3D) and coupled two-cell (6D) systems, with numerical validation.
AI.motivation: Biological intracellular calcium systems exhibit intrinsic randomness, necessitating a stochastic framework to capture natural variability; existing deterministic slow-fast ICC models do not account for such noise-driven dynamics.
AI.method: A stochastic slow-fast ICC model based on FitzHugh-Nagumo structure, analyzed first in a 3D single-cell setting and then extended to a coupled 6D two-cell system. Techniques include existence/uniqueness proofs, positivity of calcium variable, and explicit mean-square stability estimates around deterministic equilibria as functions of noise intensity.
AI.result: Existence and uniqueness of solutions are proved, positivity of the calcium variable is established, and explicit mean-square stability bounds depending on noise intensity are obtained. Numerical simulations of single-cell and coupled systems confirm qualitative behaviors and reveal additional stochastic dynamical features.
AI.conclusion: The stochastic framework provides rigorous analytical guarantees and stability quantification for ICC dynamics, extending deterministic slow-fast models and uncovering noise-induced behaviors in single and coupled cells.

title: NOC NOC, who's there? Clustering systems of tree-child and normal networks
summary:
Clustering systems provide a natural way to encode structural information contained in phylogenetic networks. In this note, we study the clustering systems of normal and tree-child networks through an overlap-based property of set systems, called not-overlap-covered (NOC). We show that the NOC property is equivalent to inclusion-visibility, a memberwise formulation of the strict-compatibility condition previously used for tree-child clustering systems.
  We characterize normal networks as precisely the semi-regular networks whose clustering systems satisfy NOC. Consequently, a clustering system is realized by a normal network if and only if it satisfies NOC, or equivalently, if every one of its clusters is inclusion-visible. In this case, the Hasse diagram provides a canonical normal realization. These are exactly the clustering systems realized by tree-child networks.
  The NOC formulation yields a sharp quadratic upper bound on the number of distinct clusters of tree-child and normal networks and a direct polynomial-time recognition algorithm. Finally, we explore several consequences of the NOC perspective beyond the phylogenetic setting. These include connections to the enumeration of normal networks, an order-theoretic interpretation of inclusion-visibility, structural properties of NOC set systems, and a tractable special case of Minimum Set Cover, which is NP-hard in general.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "not-overlap-covered" (NOC) property of clustering systems and shows it characterizes normal and tree-child phylogenetic networks, yielding algorithmic and combinatorial consequences.
